utterances.text: The way your evidence was given was to the effect that you held two-thirds of all the front line as it were, but it's a very small portion of Travnik to which you're referring, correct, of the Travnik front line?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a long front -- defence front line in the north-west of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also worth observing that this letter from Leotar is addressed to the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Battalions and it's right, isn't it, that they were fully formed by this stage of May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were administratively formed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had full complements of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in administrative terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you will answer my question. Were they, please, fully formed in military terms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In administrative terms, yes. On the ground, there were as many problems as you like, that is, setting up properly structured whole. The command personnel, because they were not fully trained, they did not have full military training so that in administrative terms, it looked fine, but in practice, things were much worse, much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So trying to understand that, you're accepting that there was a full complement of soldiers for each of these three battalions?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In administrative terms, yes, but in practice, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that there had been a build-up of Muslim troops from April of 1993, I think you told us. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in early -- on the 3rd of June, 1993, it adopted as of October 1992, they were already -- troops were being brought to the municipality of Travnik in a planed manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, and I haven't been able to check the transcript this morning, but I think when you spoke of the build-up of troops you specifically referred to the period of April of 1993 and onwards. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is that in October 1992, Alagic and Cuskic came with their two brigades, the 1st and the 7th and stationed them in that area. After that, units of the 7th Muslim Brigade and part of Mujahedin were deployed so that by June, the forces were grouped and then I listed the brigades and said that by June, about 10.000 soldiers were concentrated around Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to accept or reject your figures in detail. It's right, isn't it? You can just confirm this for the Judges. This is paragraph 26 of the summary if anybody's following it, that the 306th, the 312th, and the 17th Krajiska Brigades were all based in Travnik. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 306, 312, 17th Krajina Brigade, part of the 7th Muslim and the Mujahedin, parts of the 305th Jajce Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a sense, you forecast my next question. All the other brigades to which you refer are actually based elsewhere and, at most, I can't deal with this in any more detail, at most, may have been, in part, deployed in Travnik. You'd accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not mention the 305th, the so-called Jajce Brigade which was also deployed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now you've mentioned that brigade, is the proposition that I advanced to you correct? All these other brigades were deployed elsewhere, were based elsewhere, and insofar as they featured in Travnik, were only, in part, deployed in Travnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made some observations yesterday about comparisons of units. Would you accept that the BiH 3rd Corps, three corps, was, broadly speaking, to be matched to the Operational Central Zone of Central Bosnia of the HVO, each being of ten brigades or so in strength?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is -- I mean I know the area of the municipality of Travnik at the time. And what did the Operative Zone in the 3rd Corps head under their command, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any answers you gave about the comparative strength or the strength of the Central Operative Zone we should disregard because they're outside your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I compared, I never mentioned the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. I mentioned HVO forces and army forces in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So all we know about and all you can tell us about is the Travnik armed forces wherever they came from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forces which were stationed in the territory of the municipality of Travnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case, Your Honour, I shan't take statistics any further with this witness, save to say that the proportions he gave yesterday of eight to one are something that we don't accept, but we can't obviously take it any further, in light of his answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By June of 1993, we hear from one of the witnesses in this case, a Mr. Morsink, that there was a withdrawal of the HVO. Do you know anything about the burning of the local archives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that. But there was no withdrawal. The HVO was simply pushed back because of the major ABiH offensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to look at, in sequence, the reports from the International Community on what was happening over the few days of the 4th to the 7th of June, and I want you to tell us if they are accurate. First, it's Exhibit 1065. Now, I'll make the document available to you, Major, although it is in English. You'll see that -- it will be on the overhead projector so that the public can see it and so that the translators can -- interpreters can follow it, but it will be on your screen. It's in English. There are three paragraphs to read, starting at paragraph 14 on page 3. Remember, please, all I'm going to ask you, as a person from Travnik, is whether what the reporting officers or monitors say is accurate. "Travnik was the only area where the Croats and Muslims appeared to be working well, despite a number of fights. But on the 4th of June, the Croats evacuated Travnik to Novi Travnik, Vitez and Turbe, held by the Serbs, amid allegations of Muslim atrocities. The Muslims took control first of Travnik, then of the mountain route from Travnik to Zenica. There is evidence that the HVO deliberately withdrew the civilian Croat population from the Travnik area in an attempt to balance their 'eviction' against events in Mostar." I'll deal with it paragraph by paragraph. Do you have any disagreement with that comment of the reporting European Monitor?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree, presumably, that there were allegations of Muslim atrocities?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evidence, I already pointed out -- that is, I gave examples of such incidents and slaughters that they had committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to read the next paragraph, 15. "The evacuation of 3.500 Croats through Northern Bosnia to Croatia suggests collusion between Croats and Serbs. The imprisonment of 750 HVO in Manjaca is balanced against the release of Serb civilians from the village of Rastani, south-east of Tomislavgrad, where they had been 'held for their protection' since the conflict began. "At a top-level meeting at Celebic on the 15th of June, the Bosnian Serbs and Croats agreed to the formal exchange of properties and populations in their respective areas." Do you accept the accuracy of all that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that on the 13th of June, I was wounded and hospitalised, so that I could not know about this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last paragraph says this: "In theory, command and control of the HVO is through the normal military chain, although recent events demonstrate without doubt that the factions are far from being able to implement the cease-fire agreements signed by the two commanders-in-chief. "Controlled or uncontrolled HVO soldiers continue to prevent freedom of movement for any humanitarian aid or civilian traffic into Muslim-held areas of Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. In particular, the military police answer only to the HVO Minister of Defence Stojic and Mate Boban and are a force in the control of traffic moving through Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. "In the Novi Travnik/Vitez/Busovaca area, HVO preventing the movement of relief convoys answer only to Dario Kordic." And it makes a comment about him. Now, is there anything in that paragraph that relates to Travnik that you would disagree with? It speaks of the normal military chain, of controlled and uncontrolled HVO soldiers, and the military police answering up to Boban. True or false, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of command of the military police is something that I do not know what it looked like at the time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it was not under my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 1019.1. Is this document, although it relates -- the document you've just been looking at related to the 16th of June but, as you'll appreciate, started in its history an account of the 4th of June. This document is a military document, and it dates, more specifically, the 5th of June. So this is before you were injured -- wounded, I'm sorry. Again, I'd like your comment simply on the accuracy of it. It reads: "Further to the shelling of the civilian coaches yesterday, enquiries reveal that the convoy which was from the Merhamet Aid Agency and was not accredited to the UNHCR was en route from Austria to Tuzla." Do you have any recollection of that, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps then I can pass, unless anybody wants me to read out the balance of 1 to 2. "The convoy leader, Jasmin" -- name unknown -- "claims that yesterday the convoy was stopped at the Stojkovici checkpoint, where all the buses were searched in an aggressive manner by the HVO. One of the coaches contained medical supplies destined for Tuzla, and the HVO claimed that they were supplying Muslims with aid. Eventually, however, the convoy was permitted to proceed north. While leaving the checkpoint, the convoy leader reportedly observed an HVO soldier speaking on his radio, and then when the convoy reached the next checkpoint at the Novi Travnik T-junction, it was stopped again by members of the HVO." Further references to the vehicle being targeted. Now, do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The events mentioned here happened in a different municipality in which I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then under item 3: "The Travnik liaison officer," that's a military liaison officer, I think, "attended a meeting in the Travnik PTT building, the location of the joint HQ, in an attempt to arrange a cease-fire between the HVO and the BiH. Alagic, Merdan and Kulenovic represented the BiH and Leotar the HVO, with the major" -- I'm so sorry -- "and president of the civil government, who yesterday surrendered their authority to the military." First of all, is that correct? You were there the 5th of June. Had there been a surrender of authority to the military on the 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said I was not there. I told you that at that time I was near my command post, that is, near Polje Dolac, and there were already 12 dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about a lot of villages where things happened. You didn't see all of these yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on the period of time we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember this morning Mr. Sayers, Mr. Kordic's counsel, took you through lots of villages on a report, and you were able to give us comments on people who had been injured in these various places. You didn't visit them all yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, that area, while it was under my command, I personally visited them during that period of time, all that was under my command. When my unit was reorganised and after I was wounded, I was put in the headquarters in the command, and there was an exchange of information between the command and units. Neighbouring units, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the village of Bukovice in relation to your command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to the right from my command post towards Vlasic. My command post, Bukovice, direction of the transmitter on Vlasic, if we are talking about Velika and Maljabuka [phoen], because there is another Bukovice in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Radojcici, if I pronounce it even remotely correct; where was that in relation to your area of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojcici was not in the area. Again, it depends on what time frame we're talking about. At the time of the existence of the Frankopan Brigade, at that time, that area was not under my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same part of the report of the monitor goes on to say: "Merdan claimed that 18 Muslims had been massacred in the village of Bukovice and that something similar had happened in Radojcici." True or false, please? Had Muslims been massacred, to your knowledge, at that time? That's by the 5th of June.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it did not happen in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just complete this passage. The monitor says: "At this point, there is no collateral for either claim," and I think that means no support one way or the other for either claim. "Alagic and Leotar claim they had not discerned a precise cause for the outbreak of fighting. Nevertheless, they agreed at 1110 hours to inform their respective commands of a cease-fire which was to come into effect at 1300." And then they asked for various practical matters for that. Would you please now look at 1020 to see if this reflects the truth of the position in Travnik at the time of which you're speaking, please, and I'm afraid it's another English document. It's the fourth page of unnumbered pages, please. And it says of Travnik this: "The situation in Travnik," -- sorry, I must give you the date, Major. The date is -- recorded the date as the 6th of June. Yes, the 6th of June. So it's a report on something that's happening up to the 6th of June itself, on the 6th June itself and it says of Travnik, "The situation in Travnik remained very tense with various fire exchanges, mortar exchanges continuing in the town and the outlying villages throughout the day. The fighting was, however, less intense than yesterday. There are reports of mortar rounds being airburst over the area. Confirmed four dead in Slimena and at an HVO checkpoint ..." and it gives the reference," ... members of the checkpoint claim that they now control the previously BiH held village of Bukovice and that there are a number of dead and injured people still in that area." So I ask you again: Was there killing in Bukovice and did that lead to the HVO taking control of that village?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Bukovice at that time was no longer in my zone of responsibility and I was not familiar with its area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there was an observation of detained persons, I think, masked in the Croat village of Caravo. Do you know anything about that village? It says, "Amongst the people were approximately 200 HVO troops and the Croats of Caravo claimed that they were being fired upon from BiH positions in Turbe and that they wished to move to Nova Bila." Does that sound to you to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because of Caravo -- is north-west of Travnik, and I could not have been there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same person also observed numerous other DPs coming down from the high ground south of Travnik heading for the same village. Now, I want your comments simply on a summary of how things were in Travnik that can be found on paragraph ten, the next sheet, which reflects two meetings held by Ambassador Thebault and then the second by a commanding officer of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment, some British soldiers, a British officer. Leotar was there, and you can see the list of the other people who were present and this is the way the meet was described. "The morning meeting was not conducted in an atmosphere of mistrust but rather one of sadness that the possibility of coexistence between Croats and Muslims, which Travnik had stood for was now, is over." Does that fit with your recollection of events that, for a long time, Travnik was a possibility for coexistence but, for whatever reason, that that was no longer possible by June 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Travnik was and could have stayed an area of coexistence but in early June, in fact, at the beginning of 1993, ABiH created a lot of incidents killing a number of Croats and this affected the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're really putting it down all to one side, are you, in the Travnik area? You're not remotely accepting that the HVO, the Croat-based organisation, had any part to play in the deteriorating relationships?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do accept that the HVO had a part to play in the deteriorating relationships. If so, tell us what part it had to play.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. The HVO did not play a role in worsening the relations. It was the opposite. It did everything to try to normalise and calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then just to complete this document, because I want you to have a chance to comment on it fully, coming from Travnik, it goes on to say, "Both parties that agreed that the events in Travnik were a catastrophe for the Croats and Muslims in Province 10 as the last example of coexistence had fallen. Both sides wished for Blaskic and Hadzi Jovanovic to attend a later meeting. This was constantly reiterated. "Both Leotar and Bilandzija stated that the Croats of Travnik wished to leave the town. Bilandzija claimed they were prepared to leave all their possessions given the circumstances." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying they weren't willing to leave the town. Is that what you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about the meeting, and I am not aware that he had said this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a conclusion to have an immediate cease-fire? There were reconvened negotiations, paragraph 12, later. Your Honour, again, unless anybody wants me to read it out now, more conveniently, it can be dealt with later on and I will just turn, I think, to the last document. Perhaps it's worth looking at it together, if we may, just at the comment on the last sheet of this document as it comes up later. "The prospects for the cease-fire holding in Travnik looked remote with both sides demonstrating little faith in the motives of the other. 3 Corps, judging by the attitude of its commander, seems poised for further military action having clearly rejected the concept of negotiation. The restraining influence, at present, may well be the progress north of the large convoy destined for Tuzla as renewed fighting in the Lasva Valley east of Travnik would sever the only remaining route open to it." Major, did you know anything about that convoy bound for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in that -- at that time, I heard about this convoy, but this was a time when I was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which case then, the last document on this topic, but one I want your comment on is 1025.1. This is for the 7th of June, the day after, and quite a large entry for Travnik. I'll try and take the Court through it and the witness to it swiftly. It's paragraph three which says that the situation was calmer on the 7th, apparently free of fighting although there was fighting continuing in Dolac, Grahovice, and Slimena. Then we go to paragraph four. "A visit of Commander Leotar reported it had been complete that Jankovici had been demolished and additionally that the previously, Croat-dominated areas leading up through Travnik to the headquarters, namely the Kalbunar and Jankovici, were completely devoid of Croats." Do you accept the accuracy of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only asking you for the accuracy of the document, not the content. Do you understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you are reading this information from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting very far with this witness. He refuses to follow the question, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I am bound to say I don't disagree with that. Can I just take him, if I can find it immediately, to the particular point on this document which I want him to deal with. Just give me one minute, if that's possible. Yes. It's paragraph five, I think. I might ask the witness just to comment to see if he can or if he will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of this report from a military man says this, Major: "A normally reliable BiH source offered the following explanation of certain events in Travnik. He claimed that an order was issued by the Travnik HVO ordering the evacuation of Croats to Ovcarevo from the surrounding villages which were said to include Jankovici, Bilici, Paklarevo, Birota [phoen], Kraljenice." And he goes on to say that: "The people, including HVO soldiers who had discarded their uniforms, moved out of Ovcarevo and reputedly crossed the Serb lines to Bobanovac saying this was part of a well-organised agreement by which the HVO would surrender their positions in the defence of Travnik and Turbe to the BSA." Now, was that source of information correct, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evidence, I said that I heard from Commander Leotar that Colonel Blaskic had issued an order to protect the civilian population and to be taken to a safe area. That was in the area of Nova Bila and Novi Travnik, and specifically given the casualties, both civilians and military, I was tasked to protect the civilians in that area. The commander -- I don't know what orders were received by the commanders of the 1st and 2nd Battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or how they crossed the Serb lines. Do you know how that happened, if not by agreement with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that part. I can only speak to the area in which I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to cast your mind back, very briefly, to an early exhibit. I'm not going to ask you to have the exhibit before you, because it's not one that you'd seen although it related to the 21st of October, the day of the funeral, as you tell us, of your leader. The document was the one where Kordic and Blaskic claimed to be leading operations in the area. Your Honour, it's paragraph three that I didn't deal with, and I want the witness' comment on it. Those same people, that's Blaskic and Mr. Kordic, in their letter, said this of Ivica Stojak, his death, and negotiations. They said, "The situation in Travnik, Zenica, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Fojnica, Kresevo, Vares, and Kakanj is under complete control of the HVO, but the behaviour of the HVO military and civilian personnel in Travnik was incomprehensible. They began negotiations and arrangements for a cease-fire after the association [sic] of the commander of the Travnik command, the late Ivica Stojak ..." -- yes, assassination -- "... without the knowledge of their superior command and taking advantage of our preoccupation with the situation in Novi Travnik." Now, this is a comment about negotiations and arrangements and the local HVO military and civil personnel in Travnik. Do you accept that the local military and civilian personnel in Travnik negotiated a cease-fire without reference up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was a battalion commander and at that time, it was against BSA forces, and it was not within my competence to know what was going on in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've only got a few more documents to deal with, and I'll try to deal with them by lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you are going to say that you were injured and wounded and all, that it was out of your area of responsibility, but can you just comment on a document we looked at earlier, Z134 which I -- which was incorrectly dated. This is the 15th of June, 1993. By that time, were you an injured person, a wounded person? Were you wounded by the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain how, and you can see the document which is in your language and has got formal stamps on it over typed signatures of Blaskic and Kordic. Can you explain, please, how at that time, orders of a military nature were being given by Kordic and Blaskic, please, a battle order to the Tomasevic Brigade in Travnik. Can you explain, please, how that would happen?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the document, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course you may. 134.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see it in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you got the original on the ELMO? Can you hand the original to the witness, please. Detach it.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original says -- what you are calling the original is the 15 June, 1992. Is it 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it says 1992 but it's clear if you look at the --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you asked me about 15 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the content of the document and if you look at the serial number of the letter immediately above the date, it would appear 1992 is an error and that it's a 1993 document. I just want your comment, if you can, on how Blaskic and Kordic could be making an order of this kind.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they issued this order. As I said, on the 15th, I was wounded. That was in 1993, 15 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, frankly, I've got a number of matters that I ought to raise with the witness from Travnik, but I've got a feeling -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't see that you were discussing matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I think we better bring this to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I better bring it to a conclusion, because I don't think I'm going to get any answers from this witness, and my duty to put my case has, I hope, been sufficiently discharged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Major, about some of the documents that you were shown. First of all, Exhibit 243, which is an announcement/report on the situation in Novi Travnik and Jajce or maybe I observe that it's not actually signed, but if you would just take a look at the people to whom it was to be addressed, Major. The English translation says that the addressees are all HVO municipal headquarters of SB HB. Were those military organisations or civilian organisations, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were municipal civilian headquarters and civilian military headquarters at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was this announcement sent to the civilian bodies of the municipalities or to the military bodies of the municipalities for informational purposes or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak to it because at that time, I never received such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were asked some questions in connection with Mr. Puljic who was the chief of the Travnik Defence Administration. Is it the case that the civilian defence administration had responsibility for registering conscripts and more mobilising conscripts who would then be sent off to the army and then be subjected to the military chain of command or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the defence administration carried out the administrative aspects of the mobilisation of forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, let me just suggest to you that coming from where I come from, that is an odd concept. Let me just ask you this: With respect to Mr. Puljic, who we've identified as the chief of the Travnik defence administration, is it the case that he would report to the Minister of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Bruno Stojic, or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not fully familiar with the chain of command of the Ministry of Defence. I know that the municipal headquarters had -- that there were defence offices at the municipal level, but I don't know more specifically what the chain was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing that's confusing is you've referred to these municipal headquarters. Were they military or were they civilian organisations, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I referred to the war headquarters, those were the headquarters which were tasked with the military matters, and the municipal headquarters was engaged in civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see if we can try to clarify that by reference to one of the other exhibits about which you were asked some questions, Exhibit Z534.1. You're being shown the Croatian, sir. I wonder if the original could be put on the ELMO for everyone to see. This was an order signed by Mr. Puljic, as chief of the Travnik defence administration, dated March the 12th, 1993. But as you can see, it was to be delivered to the chiefs of municipal defence offices in Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Zenica, and Vares. Now, these municipality defence offices, sir, were these part of the civilian administration or were they within the military chain of command? Could you help us out with that, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence offices were the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. The other document that I want to ask you about is Exhibit Z193.2 concerning the anniversary celebrations of the Holy Ghost 1st Company at an uncertain date. First of all, Major, the document that is in Croatian and has some lines scratched out by someone, do you have any idea who scratched those lines out from this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Holy Ghost Company was a unit which existed for about one and a half months, so that I don't know this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just try to direct your attention to this particular document. Do you have any idea who scratched that language out and wrote in another word, "Ostrojvi", by the look of it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell whether this single page bears any relationship to the document to which it's attached, any relationship at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these two documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do they bear a relationship to one another, that you can tell?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the copy that I have, I cannot tell. But this one is referring to the Holy Ghost Company, and I already commented on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did. All right. Well, let's turn to the proposal for the ceremony, whatever date it is. If you turn to page 2 of the Croatian original -- I think it's page 2 -- under the heading of "Master of Ceremonies", paragraph 7, the first person listed there is Mr. Pero Krizanac, who would address all present. He's identified as the acting president of the Travnik HVO. Was that a civilian organisation or a military organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to Pero Krizanac. That's the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August of 1993, sir, there wasn't any Travnik HVO, was there, as far as you know; it had all been cleaned out the month before by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean August 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Travnik in August 1993, there was no civilian or military institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one other point about this. Under item 8, which is in the English headed "Security" -- I'm sorry, item 9, under the heading of the ceremony, and there's another paragraph 9 there which announces what would be announced by the master of ceremonies. First, there would be an address by the HVO Travnik president. That would be Mr. Krizanac, I take it.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when was Mr. Krizanac the president of the Travnik HVO, as far as you can recall, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Up until what time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. I don't know until what date, because I was involved in purely military affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second address is to be given by the Territorial Defence, and that was a purely Muslim military body in Travnik, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, before ABiH had that name, the name "TO" was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any swearing-in ceremonies or oath-taking ceremonies of any kind, Major, at any time where an address was given to the assembled new soldiers or people who were being sworn in by members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of questions in connection with two final documents, Major. But before I go to that, just one question. Did you ever hear that Mr. Mate Boban ever visited Travnik at any time in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Mr. Boban visited Travnik in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know that Mr. Boban visited Travnik during the wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And two final questions. In connection with one of the military information summaries you were shown, Z1019.1, dated June the 5th of 1993 -- I don't think that it's necessary, Mr. Usher, to show the document; let me just read from it. There's a reference on page 2 to the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, stating that he had little faith in diplomacy and the political process. And then another individual by the name of Suvalic stated that: "Muslims felt cheated and disappointed by the International Community and were being left with little alternative to military action to resolve matters." And the comment is made that: "Although neither party would be drawn on the question of what was to be the next step, the unavoidable conclusion was that the BiH were no longer prepared to restrain themselves and were likely to take the military initiative in the Lasva Valley, where they enjoy a tactical advantage over the HVO." Did you ever hear, Major, that General Hadzihasanovic was at this time refusing to meet with Colonel Blaskic to try to resolve differences without fighting?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At my level, I did not hear about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just see if I can jog your memory on that -- maybe I can't -- with Exhibit 1020, and this is the last question I have for you. You were not asked about paragraph 12 of this British military information summary dated June the 6th of 1993, but here is what it says: "Negotiations reconvened at 1800 but without the planned attendance of Blaskic and Hadzihasanovic. Blaskic had been willing to attend, but Hadzihasanovic, despite the intervention of BHC, maintained his previous position by stating that it was now too late for negotiation. He claimed that he had the full support of General Halilovic for the position he was adopting." And then there are some other comments made. Does that ring a bell? Do you have any recollection of General Hadzihasanovic refusing to attend negotiations with Colonel Blaskic and claiming that it was too late for negotiations?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Ljubas, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to go. You are released. We will adjourn for an hour and a half, until 2.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.10 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson is unwell. He has the flu of some sort and therefore cannot sit this afternoon. Unless there's any objection, we propose to make an order under the usual Rule, 15, for the two of us to sit, and we hope he will be back tomorrow but he may not be of course. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I will make the order. Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Civcija. Mr. Civcija, will you please give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: My name is Zlatan Civcija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, you were born in Travnik in 1954, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Croat by ethnicity and a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina and you lived in Novi Travnik for some 40 years until 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Currently, you and your family live in the town of Grahovo which is the southwestern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you work as a legal advisor by a public company called Sume?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, however, between April 1996 and September 1997, you were a provisional administrator in the town of Grahovo which is something like appointed designated mayor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, will you please pause after you have heard my questions to give time to the interpreters. Thank you. And after you stopped being this designated mayor until March this year, you were deputy mayor of Grahovo; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for your education, you graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo in 1980 and worked as a lawyer for the weapons factory, Bratstvo, in Novi Travnik for some ten years. For a while you were a lawyer there and then you were the head, the manager of joint affairs of those departments, as those matters used to be called then.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, that is before the civil war broke out, you became the chief of the Novi Travnik police, and I would call it the chief or rather perhaps the head because it was an administrative duty, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: The exact name of that post which I took up in March, I believe, 1990, is the chief of the public security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the police station in Novi Travnik, you stayed with the civilian police until 28th September 1993, and at that time you joined the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade of the Croat Defence Council in Novi Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You joined the HVO, that is the above-mentioned brigade, as a platoon commander and as a platoon commander that is a member of the HVO. You did that until the end of the civil war between the Muslims and the Croats, that is, you were at the front lines until sometime in the spring 1994.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more fact about your career. In 1995, you worked at the Ministry of the Interior of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I'd like to ask Mr. Civcija what his current occupation is. What is he doing right now? What does he do or what has his job been from 1995 onwards until today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand the question asked by His Honour, Judge Bennouna?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, and I should like to answer that question. As the counsel has already said, in 1995 I worked for the Ministry of the Interior of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar. From April of 1996 to some time late 1997, I was a government-responsible agent for the municipality of Bosanski Grahovo. After the last municipal elections, I was appointed deputy mayor of the municipality of Bosanski Grahovo and head of the department of economic affairs, and I held that post until sometime in March this year. And then in early April, we had new local elections and I was the first on the HDZ list. We have not yet appointed the new local government in the municipality of Bosanski Grahovo. It was due one of these days. And meanwhile, I have begun to work for the public company Sume Forests. It is a cantonal enterprise engaged in forestry exploitation and preservation of forests, and there I have the job of legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on, Mr. Civcija. Just a few general facts about the municipality of Novi Travnik. According to the census of 1991, in the municipality of Novi Travnik, there were about 12.500 Croats, which is some 40 per cent, and there was slightly less Muslims, 11.600, which is some 38 per cent of the total. There were also 16 per cent of Serbs and a few percentage points of other people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: I believe these figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These three ethnic groups, three peoples, which lived in the town of Novi Travnik, by and large respected customs and traditions of other groups, that is, they were all more or less on good terms, and yet nevertheless each one of those ethnic groups was more or less separate and lived its own life, and this especially holds true of rural environments; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so. About a third of the population or some 10.000 of the inhabitants lived in the town, and two thirds, that is, some 20.000, lived principally in villages and small localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those ethnic groups, that is, peoples in the former Yugoslavia, in the old regime prior to 1990, were privileged as opposed to other peoples. Could you tell Their Honours, what was that people and how did these privileges manifest themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The former State of Yugoslavia was a federal state, that is, a composite state made of six republics and two provinces. In that state, the majority people were the Serbs, and, in a manner, they enjoyed some privileges when compared with other peoples, because they largely controlled the army -- I believe that about 90 per cent of the officers were Serbs -- the police, public sector, that is, public companies. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other two peoples, Muslims and Croats, at the time that you are talking about, were somewhat discriminated against by virtue of the functions in those institutions that you have just mentioned. You are well acquainted with the structure, because that is one of the things that you did, the structure of the police command for which you worked for a while in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One people there was completely neglected?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. For a long time, the predominant people at all leading positions in the police were the Serbs, so that both the Croats and Muslims were discriminated against; notably, especially the Croats, because they were the smallest people in terms of the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the executive posts in the police in 1989 and in 1990, the central government in Sarajevo tried to compensate for this lack of Croats in executive posts in the police, and some Croats were then, including yourself, appointed to individual duties in some police stations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In 1989 and 1990, throughout Yugoslavia, was the period of the democratisation of the state, in view of the changes taking place in neighbouring countries. By this, I mean the countries of the Socialist Eastern Bloc. Even though Yugoslavia was one of the more liberal states, if one can put it that way, when compared with this Socialist Bloc, it was nevertheless a state with only one political party. And by Western standards, it could not be defined as a democratic state, therefore. With the fall of the Berlin Wall and the relaxation of discipline in the Soviet Union, this process also expanded to our country, and it was manifest in different ways. One of the aspects of this was to try to redress the injustice in the police, army, and other places concerning one people, so that in my republic, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the head of the police stations in several places, about a dozen Croats were appointed, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, in November 1990, the first multi-party elections took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in all the municipalities, and that includes the municipality of Novi Travnik. In the elections, in the local elections in Novi Travnik, the chief political party of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, won the largest number of seats, and it was followed by the Party for Democratic Action, that is, the chief Muslim party, and then others. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in line with the election results, the new government was also conceived, and offices were distributed between the parties, so that a Croat became a mayor of the municipality, and a Muslim the president of the local government, to put it in that matter, and then the representative of the third largest people, the Serbs, he became the secretary of the municipal government, and so on and so forth. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this distribution of offices, the Croats were allotted the place of the civil police, so that you continued in the job that you already held, but this time in agreement of all the parties in the municipality of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, however, the head of the police covering the administrative field. Your deputy was a Muslim, and he was involved with the active part of the police.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few questions, Mr. Civcija -- and we have reached paragraph 9, Your Honours -- a few questions about the developments in the Republic of Croatia in the latter half of 1991. At the time when you -- and by this I mean the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- watched on television and in other media to follow the war that was raging in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, how did you see that, and did you begin to think about what might happen to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: The war operations in 1991 in Slovenia and then in Croatia gave rise to concern -- to anxiety among all the peoples who lived in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially the Croats, because they could daily see on their small screens the horrible images of war, the shelling of Vukovar, of Dubrovnik, of Zadar, and a number of other places across the Republic of Croatia, and this caused grave concern to the Croat community in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you saw raging already in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, did it make you also begin to think -- begin to consider your own defence, the defence of your own lands in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Well, we realised that after a long time of the existence of Yugoslavia, which was, however you look at it, a dictatorship. The time had come for it to fall apart, to be dissolved, so that all the constituent factors which made Yugoslavia should be given their own states. We saw it happen with Slovenia, with Croatia, with Macedonia, and it was natural to expect that Bosnia-Herzegovina would become a state too. When I say "state", I mean an internationally-recognised state. And in that sense, we also began to carry out certain preparations for that act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was certain developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when some Croat villages and localities were victimised. However, other peoples did not react identically. Could it be that at that time between you, the Croats, and members of other peoples, that is, Muslims, there were already some misunderstandings, some divergences as to what might happen? Did the leadership of Bosnian Muslims, and also speaking from the point of view of Novi Travnik, were they on the same wavelength with you Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Since you're asking me this, I will point out the village of Ravno which is in the southeastern corner of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we were unpleasantly surprised by the response of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina when the village of Ravno was attacked by the JNA and the Serb paramilitary troops which shelled this village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber already heard what happened in the village of Ravno. We do not have to go into any details. But if I understand you correctly, on the other side, among the Muslims, there was no concern and there was no concern among the Muslim leadership in terms of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: This is what I could -- how I could answer this question. The Muslim political leadership believed that it would be able to get the independence and that the guarantor of that would be the JNA. They did not understand what at first befell Slovenia then Croatia, to a larger degree, and then what was to befall Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking about the preparations of the Bosnian Croats, you will agree with me that thousands of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the Croatian army which was amassing at the time in order to assist Croatia in defending its boarders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the JNA carried out emigration against the Republic of Croatia and many people, young and old, I believe some 15.000 of them from Bosnia and Herzegovina, went to Croatia to defend its sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia resulted in a cease-fire, most of these people went back home in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, many went back and talked about the horrors which they experienced because it was not possible to get all the information from television, so the testimonies of the people who took part in the defence of Croatia were really moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand but these same people, when the civil war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, came back to defend their own homes so now they were taking part in another war, in a second war at home.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely right. It is also logical that people who went to defend Croatia should come back home to defend their own homes. They came back immediately and did everything they could to defend the areas where they were born and the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the town where you spent all your life, 40 years, most of your life, there was a very significant factory called Bratstvo. It was a military factory. Materiel from this and weapons from this factory were sent to -- was used by the JNA to wage the war in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: When the events in Croatia took place, people responded with fear. They expressed their discontent and bitterness, but the situation was further exacerbated by the fact that our own neighbours and kin were being attacked with the weapons produced in our own factory. And we wanted to do something to prevent and stop this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But because people of all ethnic groups worked in the factory, but the Croats and Muslims differed on what to do. The Croats wanted to prevent the weapons from being used against Croatia, and the Muslims wanted it to keep working because they wanted the economic benefit, but the only use of that was for the war in Croatia so this is where you differed.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. But this is how I would put this. There was an attempt on the part of the factory management who made decisions about the deliveries of weapons. They wanted to represent that they were forced by economic reasons to deliver weapons to the JNA which was not correct. And politically speaking, the representatives of Muslims who adopted -- didn't see this trick, if I can call it that. The JNA aimed at getting out all the weapons and equipment from the factory and warehouse in their own depots. They had enough weaponry and equipment, but it was important for them that the other side did not have any. So this is why they wanted it out, but the political leadership of Muslims did not see this trap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bratstvo factory was part of the military industrial complex, and the management consisted of the former JNA officers or trusted people, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely. And in order to explain what -- how it was, from the establishment of the factory until the end, until the beginning of war that is, the manager could not be anybody who was not a former officer of the JNA. And the top management had to be JNA officers which means that 99 per cent of them were of Serbian ethnic background. And of course, as soldiers, they carried out orders of their superiors who were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite these differences in views between you and Muslims, and despite all the deliveries of weapons, you were able to stop and prevent some of this weaponry from reaching the JNA. However, did you not keep those weapons for yourselves only. You received an order or a decision to share it with the Muslims. Do you know who passed this decision or who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Frankly, Croats, as an ethnic group in Novi Travnik, on several occasions, barred transports of weapons from leaving the compound. And on one occasion, they even took some weapons because the war was approaching the boarders of Bosnia and we were under a real threat of being attacked. All weapons which, at that time, we stopped, we divided into two equal parts. I think this order came from the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think the Defence minister at the time was Mr. Jerko Doko, and I also heard that Mr. Stjepan Kljuic, who was a member of the Presidency, also became involved in this, and I attended some of these meetings. And we implemented this decision from the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo and distributed the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Doko were members of the top leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, you know of many cases of distribution of weapons, at least this is what paragraph 13 refers to. You shared with the other side, with the Muslims, the weapons which was in the Bratstvo factory which was to have been used as -- for air defence. You did not keep those weapons but rather you shared it with the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said in the beginning, Bratstvo was a military factory and they all had a certain type of security. Part of that security system in the Bratstvo factory were anti-aircraft guns which were kept at Bratstvo, and for 40 or 50 years of its existence, there was always a crew which was trained to use these weapons. We divided these anti-aircraft guns equally between the Croatian and Muslim groups when we started preparing against the aggression of the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move swiftly through the next segment. You also shared weapons, the weapons seized from the JNA in the facility in Stojkovici and from the Slimena facility, and even the weapons from the municipal sports club which was used for rifle-shooting, and all the weapons that remained in the army barracks after the retreat of the JNA. And you shared all those weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I personally took part in the distribution of weapons we had seized in Stojkovici, and Mr. Filipovic, who at that time, I believe, was a colonel, was present there and with my colleague in the police force, I personally distributed weapons that the municipal sports club used to have. And I took part in the transport of weapons to the Muslims alongside Mr. Cengic. I believe on two occasions, there was 24 truckloads which we took to Visoko and these weapons were successfully used in the defence of the city of Sarajevo which was already under the attack of the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs. I believe that it was thanks to those weapons that the city of Sarajevo was defended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this convoy to Visoko, the 24 truckloads. You personally escorted this convoy and you were involved in providing security for it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One of the chief logistics persons in the Bosniak armed forces was Mr. Cengic, and I assumed that from one of the top leaders or the -- in the central government in Bosnia, he was tasked with coming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, I'm going to interrupt you. Mr. Civcija, we've heard a lot of evidence in this case about these events, and I think it would help if we could get on to the more relevant parts. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We can move on, Mr. Civcija. We are at paragraph 14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard that on the 29th of February and 1st of March, 1992, a referendum was held in order to decide the issue of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps we should touch on this issue quickly. The question was how the question in the referendum was phrased. This is, again, where you and the Muslim side differed. There were only 17.4 per cent Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and as a minority group, you wanted some guarantees for an equal status that you used to have in the previous Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. The issue of the independence is one of the key issues, how the future community is going to be organised. Both Croats and Muslims were in favour of independence, but even before this referendum on independence, we wanted to build in some safety mechanisms so that the minority group would be guaranteed its rights, so that it be a fully-constituent group, so that it could be equal, so that it would not be outvoted. There were certain doubts and misunderstandings within the leadership on both sides, but at the referendum on whether we wanted an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, an internationally-recognised state, a majority of both of these ethnic groups voted. And thanks to their votes, this country became independent. And I want to point out that without the Croat votes, the independence would never have been voted, whereas the majority of the Serbian population never voted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, you know perfectly well that we've heard a lot of witnesses who came to testify as to the issue of how this new State of Bosnia and Herzegovina came to be. I think it would be a waste of time to return to those facts at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree, Your Honour. But this was just introductory questions, and I move on right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, to speed things along, despite the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared an independent state, basically a month later the war broke out because the army of Bosnian Serbs started a series of military offensives throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just say, in brief, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this first wave of attacks of the JNA and the BSA, hundreds of thousands -- several hundred thousand Muslims and some Croats were driven out of the north-eastern and north-western areas, and many of them went to Central Bosnia, including your area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I would like to point out that the first refugee convoy with women and children started out from the city of Sarajevo. There were about 10.000 of them, and the Serbs kept them for two or three days in Ilidza and mistreated them. Then in May and June, further convoys throughout North-western Bosnia, Eastern Bosnia, and in the municipalities of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and the whole Lasva Valley, there were floods of people, men, women, and children, who were catching different transports to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In spite of this sudden aggression and this fierce attack, the HVO, regardless of the state of organisation, the state that they were in, started to prepare for defence, and you were a bit better prepared than the Muslim side in this spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I pointed it out at the beginning. We recognised the threat which was coming, and we could see that this scenario from Slovenia and Croatia was about to be repeated and we started preparing ourselves. It is true that at that time we were a bit better prepared than our partners from the Muslim ethnic group. We offered resistance, and we went out in the field to prevent the attacks of the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. You talked about a number of refugees which came to your area, but you had other problems. Every village, every hamlet, had their own military units that were not well coordinated among themselves, which further complicated the issue, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This was a very complicated situation. In this period, we got a state, Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was in a very strange condition. It did not have its own army. In its own territory, there were units of another country. Nobody knew how to resolve this problem. Some officials from the top leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina were not aware of the danger that this army was posing, and we know that this was -- it was 99 per cent Serbian -- and did not recognise the threat. So what happened was we were attacked by this army. In our attempt to defend ourselves from this army and from the army of Bosnian Serbs, the Croatian Defence Council was formed, both the military and civilian side. This process was very painful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need for this general evidence, Mr. Naumovski. We've heard this, if I may say, time and again. We don't need general political speeches. We want this witness's evidence specifically about what he knows; namely, Novi Travnik. Let's move on, if we can, to 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We were just moving to the situation in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, talking about this mass influx of refugees from Eastern and North-western Bosnia, when they arrived, a very delicate demographic balance was upset, the demographic structure was changing dramatically, and this affected the town of Novi Travnik too.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The population doubled and tripled in size, so that there were two or three times more Muslims than before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This mass influx of refugees actually also produced a state of lawlessness. The police were unable to act in the usual way, that is, they could not keep things under control in the town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: I said that the situation was very complicated. There were more and more units and people wearing military uniforms that were passing through, and it was very difficult to control the situation, regardless of whether these were the HVO members or members of its equivalent Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to all these groups and individuals who were there, you would know, wouldn't you, as a person who was working for the police, that a number of people who had been convicted and who had been detained, people of criminal pasts who were supposed to be kept in those institutions, were released, and they also came to this area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. A number of people who were serving sentences or awaiting their trials came to this area, and it was very difficult to control all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After May 1992, there were two armies in Novi Travnik; there was the TO, which was organised in the way it was, but there was also a separate HOS unit. And these units, the units which consisted of Croats and those which consisted of Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try and speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- they harassed people of Novi Travnik, which further complicated the relations between Muslims and Croats. Were you still able to reach any types of agreements, how to organise your coexistence with the Muslims, or were these agreements simply not there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: There were two types of problems; how to establish the military and how to establish cooperation between the two sides, and how to establish cooperation between the two civilian sides. We had a crisis staff which tried to assume the role of the local municipal government which had ceased to operate. But even that didn't work out, because members of the Serbian ethnic group left those institutions, and so it was very difficult to reach any type of consensus of the two sides that remained in government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move right along to paragraph 21. Because this Crisis Staff was inefficient and unable to maintain order in Novi Travnik, the government of the HVO was established.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to tender an exhibit at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D219/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a decision on the appointment of the head of the office in the municipality of Novi Travnik. It is what Mr. Civcija just talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, this document which was signed in Mostar on the 23rd of July, 1992, it was signed by Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: No, this document was not taken on the 3rd of July but on the 13th of June. It was merely written out on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so, that is what it says. But the HVO was set up as a provisional measure in order to try to somehow organise life in Novi Travnik; is that so? So will you please tell the Court, the representatives of what people were members of this HVO government?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Croats and Muslims participated in this government. For instance, Mr. Enes Sehic, an economist, who before that was the head of a building company and manager of a bank, he was appointed head of the Department of Economic Affairs. Mr. Feriz Rizvic became a member of the government, and Mr. Safet Koco, who was a mechanical engineer, was also appointed to the government of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were Muslim representatives?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, even after the HVO was set up, all the problems were not resolved, and did the HVO seek some way to deepen their relations with the Muslims, to see why some proposal that came from your side was not acceptable, or did it all go in a completely different direction?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Well, our intention was to organise the life in this space at the time of the aggression which had already begun against this area, because shells had already begun to fall. We were attacked from aircraft, the factory was attacked as a target, the town was being attacked, there was a major influx of refugees, and we were expecting this government to begin to function, that is, ensure livelihood for the largest part of the population. However, this was accompanied by huge problems. We met on various occasions, trying to regulate our relations and see how to make that government work, but it all was an uphill battle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So in spite of the fact that the representatives of the Muslims were incorporated in this HVO government that we are talking about, some Muslim politicians nevertheless organised a parallel, if I may put it that way, war presidency consisting of Muslims only, and they, in a way, took over the management of the municipal territory mostly inhabited by the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. These are people who were hard-liners, and they must have been following somebody's instructions. They merely dodged cooperation and they set up a parallel government in the area they believed to be controlling, and that was approximately the area with the majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court two or three names of those persons, of those Muslim politicians that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Salih, who was the president of the SDA at the time, and before that he was the president of the local government, Salih Krnjic. And I think that another one's name was -- oh, it slips my mind now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ragib Zukic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Ragib Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So let us move on, and that is to the first conflict which took place on the 19th of July, 1991. If we may -- June, sorry, excuse me, June 1991. If we may, Your Honours, we heard from the Prosecutor and we also had a city map, and our witness has added some facilities which were missing from this map. We blew it up, and if we may, we should like to put it on the ELMO and ask the witness to explain, as briefly as possible, what happened where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, from now on it would be better if you didn't lead the witness. Let him give his own evidence about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honours. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, we can see this town plan, if I may call it that, and you drew there some buildings, some facilities which were missing. So could you please, as briefly as possible, explain to the Court who caused the conflict in June 1992 and what were the directions of the attack and so on so forth, but please, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
