utterances.text: Well, in a nutshell, it was like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can also use the pointer on the ELMO to point what you intend to show. You need to show it there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I understand. At that time, the commander of the Muslim army in the municipality of Novi Travnik was Mr. Mufet Lendo from a member of the Yugoslav People's Army. He is a hard-liner who was not very cooperative, and we were unable to reach an agreement with him for the two components to cooperate jointly in our operations against the army of Bosnian Serbs. He was pursuing a rather hard line, politically, and he simply wanted to command all the forces in the municipality in Novi Travnik. On the 19th of June, there was an attempt to take over the principal facilities in the town. As you can see here [indicates], the town spreads in a north/south direction. The northern entrance is next to the Mali Raj outlet where there is a junction. And on the other side, which is the fire brigade centre, this is leading to the Bratstvo factory which is two or three kilometres away. That morning, they wanted to set up a checkpoint at the -- checkpoint at the junction next to the Mali Raj, and they used an air gun. However, several members of the armed formations of the HOS, which are the Croat Defence forces, they simply pushed them away without even outside use of force. They drove them away with their noise and by making dins simply. And then late in the afternoon, that same day, the gunfire started in the town and later on I learned that the following facilities had been attacked [indicates]. The building of the police which also housed the commander of the Territorial Defence, that is the Muslim forces, then the building of the post office which they took, and the building of the school which they took. Fire was opened against the workers and the municipal hall, and the headquarters of the Croat Defence Council which is the military staff of the army of the Croats. They took the intersection and the fire brigade centre and blocked the road towards Bratstvo, and it was proceeded by an attack on the building of the HVO military police which was on the road, on the local hill, and the task of which was to protect the headquarters from this side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just slow down to make the work easier for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: I apologise. If necessary, I shall repeat it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I don't think you have to, the transcript has it all. Just try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: After that the Croat Defence Council, rather, people who happened on the positions, prevented members of the Territorial Defence to take these facilities and most of these tanks were repulsed. And in the PTT buildings, some 20 members of the TO were captured who surrendered and the building, the police building, was also turned over around there. They took to their heels so that they left the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. The school was also defended and the municipal hall and the workers' centre. The only thing that was kept under control was this intersection by the fire brigade centre, and this school which I did not show which is on the Omladinska Street and which is up in the southwestern part of the municipality. And yet another facility very important which was attacked [indicates] was the firing range. The shooting range which belonged to the town and which is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, that day, if I understood you properly, numerous facilities, the most important places in the town were attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. That day, the commander of the Territorial Defence, Mr. Lendo, issued the orders to take the most important points in that town reckoning that if he kept them under control, that it would be controlling the whole town; however, this action was thwarted. The Croat Defence Council demonstrated strength, it was more successful and they were driven out from all -- the members of the TO were driven out from all those facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, during the fighting then, were you informed that in the workers' centre there was a meeting underway between Muslim and Croat representatives?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, these meetings were taking place very frequently in the workers' centre, but also the party premises both of the HDZ and the SDA and also of the Serb Democratic Party were in the building, so that meetings were frequent there. And when the gunfire abated slightly, it was the end of the day, I personally went to see who was in the building. Maybe it was dusk, lights had not come up yet, and I heard noise and melee and I couldn't recognise people there and as I was coming out of that building, I saw Mr. Salih Krnjic, who was the local politician, a member of the Muslim people, and a HOS member who was treating him rather roughly, pulling at him and threatening to do something to him. And then I grabbed him by his arm. I simply protected him against this HOS soldier, and I drove him in my vehicle to a part of the town which was safe. In the morning, when the gunfire stopped, Mr. Colonel Filipovic -- I turned over Salih to Colonel Filipovic. From what I knew, he then took him to the new headquarters of the Territorial Defence and then he was exchanged for the president of the HVO, Mr. Jozo Senkic, who was, the next day, intercepted by the members of the Muslim army at this place, at this intersection by the fire brigade centre, and took them to the village of Kasapovici, which is to the west of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, where did you take Mr. Salih Krnjic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: I took him to the northern part of the town where there was no fighting, and I put him up temporarily in a coffee shop called "Grand".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I proceed, could I get the number for this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is D220/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, just one question more, perhaps two related to the June conflict. This June conflict in 1992 was one of the first armed conflicts between the Muslim -- between Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia. Could you tell us, was the situation informal or other as a citizen of Novi Travnik? How did you see the situation after the conflict? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, I need to say that this conflict unfortunately took place. Something that I could never expect took place. As a citizen of that town, somebody who's spent all his life in the town, I could never expect that. After that, the situation deteriorated seriously, meaning that people lost trust. And then an activity started to try to move people out of a part of the town where they did not feel the safest to another part of the town and vice versa. And I must say that this situation was also contributed to by a major look of discipline amongst the members of all armed formations and members of the people. A larger number of members, of units both in the Croat Defence Council and in the Muslim armed forces, lacked discipline, and a large number of them were punished. There were all sorts of outbursts of incident, harassment of citizens. And in such a complex situation, citizens themselves decided where they might -- they would feel safer and they began to withdraw to the parts of the town where they believed to be safer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for the reasons that you have just given us, the town of Novi Travnik, after the June conflict, was even -- informally, but it was divided into two parts, we could say so.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes. It was divided and it has remained so almost to this day, even today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us hurry on. Paragraph 27, Your Honours. Mr. Civcija, you spent a major part of your career with the civilian police. In 1991 and early 1992, the civilian police could more or less perform its duties without any particular obstruction like any other civil police the world over?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course the Novi Travnik police carried out its duties normally in 1990 and in 1991 until spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it that changed in the work of the civilian police after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: As I have mentioned, when it comes to that period of time, I said that the situation had grown very complex because there were very many members of all sorts of units in uniforms who were all in a small area. In time, the police lost the purpose and the sense and the role that they should play as the civilian police on the one hand. On the other hand, never-ending attacks by the Serb aggressor made us engage a large number of civilian policemen to join the armed forces, the military forces, and go on to the defence lines against the army of Bosnian Serbs, that is the JNA, so that members of the civilian police were involved there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the civilian police during this period of time, especially as of spring, 1992 onward, did the civilian police in Novi Travnik have any jurisdiction or control over all those military units, rather members of armies, that committed crimes in the territory of Novi Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The civilian police never had any jurisdiction of any member of any unit, whichever unit. As I already said, unfortunately at that time, some ugly things happened. There were numerous incidents, numerous outbursts. There were even several murders, evictions. I believe there was two or three cases of murder where a Croat killed a Muslim. There were also cases when a Muslim killed a Serb. There were cases where a Muslim killed a Muslim or a Croat killed a Croat. Whatever the case, it was -- they were members of some military units and they were very difficult to control. Not only did the civilian police have no jurisdiction over them, but I am quite positive that not even the members of the military police managed at that time to keep the members of military units under control or discipline on side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections, the civilian police in the town of Novi Travnik was mixed, that is, consisted of members of different peoples. How long did Muslim policemen stay with the police station or, rather, when did they simply leave and how did they do that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Well, in point of fact, I say -- I can say that it was until the first conflict that -- that is until the 19th of June, 1992 or rather they came, several members of the Muslim policemen continued to come to work for several days after that, but then somebody ordered them not to come and they simply left the police station and set up their own police station which was then housed in the part of the town controlled by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, they not only parted company with you, it was not only that the local government split up, but even the civilian police parted company and set up in two different parts of the town; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was one of the episodes during that period of time which happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. In mid-1992, the civil part of the HVO separated from the military wing and set up the office of the civil police in Travnik, rather, the civil police administration in Travnik, in other words. Tell us, please, in just two words, about something about that office. The police administration in Travnik was responsible for the whole of the Lasva Valley, that is, several municipalities. So it was also responsible for the municipality of Novi Travnik. It was the higher instance with reference to all your police stations in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it was the regional police organisation. We can call it that with a seat in Travnik. In addition to this administration with a seat in Travnik, there was also another administration in Zepce, Livno, and in Mostar. As for the police administration in Travnik, it covered several municipalities; Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Fojnica, Kiseljak, Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno. I believe I haven't omitted any of them. And it became operative sometime in mid-1992 and it had its seat in Travnik first in the music school, and then in the building of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one detail. So at the municipal level, there were civil police stations. At the regional level, there were police administrations and who was above them and who was above the police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Above them was the Department of the Interior with a seat in Mostar, with the head of the department being Mr. Vasic. He was a member of the government of the Croat Defence Council as the minister, as the head of the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to adduce my last exhibit for Mr. Civcija, a very short document. Could the usher please help us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if the usher would, thank you, and we'll then adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, yes. Just one minute more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D21/1 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript -- D221; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] It is only for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Civcija, this is the decision signed by the head of the Internal Affairs Department. Subsequently it became the ministry in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it became the ministry. That is, Mr. Branko Kvesic, he decided that you should be appointed the chief of the police station in Novi Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the explanation says that your appointment, that your -- you were nominated by the head of the police department in Travnik. That is the body which is your -- the body superior to you in administrative terms; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. -- the chief of the police department in Travnik was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Civcija. Your Honours, I believe this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Would you please be back at 9.30 to continue your evidence tomorrow. Would you remember this during the adjournment: not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and of course don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include members of the Defence team of lawyers. Could you be back, please, at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
